analysis.one_liner: Bars credit bureaus from selling homebuyers' credit reports to rival lenders without the buyer's consent.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 93 cosponsors from both parties, but the House Financial Services Committee never acted on it and it died when Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: When you apply for a mortgage, the credit bureau pulls your credit report, and other lenders can buy word that you are shopping, then bombard you with calls and offers — these are called trigger leads. The bill would stop credit bureaus from handing your report to a third party for a mortgage deal unless that lender has your documented consent, or already has a relationship with you: it made your loan, services it, or is your bank or credit union holding your account. It never got past a committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: Homebuyers and refinancers, who would stop having their credit-pull sold to competing lenders that then flood them with unsolicited calls and offers. Existing lenders the consumer already chose also benefit from less poaching.

how_it_helps.text: A credit bureau could no longer furnish a consumer's report to a third party for a mortgage deal based solely on that party's request — the practice behind trigger-lead solicitation calls.
Third parties could still get the report only if they certify the consumer's consent, originated the current loan, service it, or are an insured bank or credit union holding the consumer's account.

analysis.who_pays: Credit bureaus would lose revenue from selling trigger-lead data, and lenders who rely on buying those leads to find customers would lose their main prospecting channel.

drawbacks.text: The carve-out for insured banks and credit unions that already hold the consumer's account lets those institutions keep getting the data without fresh consent, giving them an advantage over independent lenders who would need documented consent.
If fewer lenders can find borrowers through trigger leads, some shoppers could see less competition on rates and fees — the trade-off defenders of the current practice point to.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The consumer protection is real but narrow: it targets one annoying and privacy-invading sales practice rather than the mortgage market's larger costs. The main cost is that big banks with existing customer relationships keep the information access that independent mortgage lenders would lose, which could tilt the market toward banks. On balance it helps homebuyers' privacy more than it hurts them, but it is a modest fix.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Financial Services Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never voted on it, and it expired when the 118th Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on February 7, 2024 by Rep. John Rose with nine original cosponsors from both parties, and was referred the same day to the House Committee on Financial Services.
It attracted 93 cosponsors, split 42 Democrats and 51 Republicans, but no further action was taken beyond the committee referral before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Credit bureaus and lenders that buy mortgage trigger leads kept the status quo, since the restriction was never enacted.

for.name: Rep. John W. Rose
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Financial Services Committee.

for.name: Rep. Ritchie Torres
for.what_they_did: Joined as an original cosponsor at introduction.

against.name: House Financial Services Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Patrick McHenry (R-OH)
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a markup or vote on the bill after it was referred; no action is recorded for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was genuinely split — 42 Democrats and 51 Republicans signed on — and there is no recorded floor opposition; the bill simply never advanced in committee.

industries.note: Bureaus earn fees selling trigger-lead access to mortgage shoppers' credit files. The bill would cut off that revenue by requiring documented consumer consent before a report is furnished to a third party.

industries.industry: Mortgage lead buyers and lead-generation firms
industries.note: These lenders and brokers rely on trigger leads as their main way to reach people shopping for mortgages. Losing access would force them to find customers through other channels.

industries.industry: Banks and credit unions with existing customer relationships
industries.note: The bill exempts insured banks and credit unions holding the consumer's account, so they keep getting reports without fresh consent while independent lenders need documented authorization. That protects their information access and reduces poaching of their borrowers.
